title: Cross-Departmental Architecture and Shared Platforms
objectives: Navigate the complexities of cross-departmental architecture work
Leverage GOV.UK shared platforms effectively in your architecture
Engage with the Technical Design Council and Enterprise Architecture team
Design for interoperability using government open standards
Manage the governance, politics, and practicalities of cross-government delivery
whyThisMatters:
No government service exists in isolation. Citizens interact with multiple departments, data flows between systems across organisational boundaries, and policy outcomes often depend on services delivered by several organisations working together. Yet government is structured in departmental silos — each with its own technology estate, its own standards, its own procurement, and its own priorities.

The Blueprint for Modern Digital Government sets out a vision of joined-up public services. The GDS Enterprise Architecture team works to elevate harmonisation, interoperability, and reuse across the public sector. GOV.UK One Login, GOV.UK Notify, GOV.UK Pay, and the GOV.UK app are shared platforms designed to be used across departments. The Technical Design Council makes decisions affecting cross-government architecture.

But the reality of cross-departmental work is hard. Different departments have different technology stacks, different security classifications, different risk appetites, and different political priorities. Getting three departments to agree on an API standard is genuinely difficult. Getting them to share data requires legal gateways, data protection impact assessments, and technical integration. This lesson prepares you for that reality.

content.heading: The Cross-Government Architecture Landscape
content.body:
Cross-government architecture operates through several mechanisms that have evolved significantly since the Blueprint for Modern Digital Government was published in January 2025.

The Technical Design Council (TDC) is the senior decision-making body for cross-government architecture. Composed of empowered Chief Technology Officers from across the public sector, the TDC is responsible for decisions affecting cross-government architecture and shared platforms. It uses Architecture Decision Records as its decision mechanism — proposals are submitted as ADRs, debated, and either accepted or returned. The TDC sits within the governance structure established by the Blueprint.

The GDS Enterprise Architecture team, relaunched in late 2025 within the Office of the Chief Technology Officer (OCTO), provides strategic direction, expert guidance, and architectural coherence across the public sector. Their focus is on harmonisation, interoperability, and reuse — helping teams design and deliver services that are joined-up, scalable, and user-centred. They maintain architecture resources and capability models that departments can use.

The Open Standards Board selects open standards for government technology. These mandated standards ensure interoperability — if all departments use the same standards for data exchange, their systems can communicate without bespoke integration for each pair. Selected standards cover areas like document formats, character encoding, data interchange, and persistent resolvable identifiers.

Government shared platforms provide common capabilities that departments should use rather than building their own. GOV.UK One Login provides authentication and identity verification. GOV.UK Notify sends emails, text messages, and letters. GOV.UK Pay processes payments. GOV.UK Forms provides a form-building capability. The GOV.UK app brings government services to mobile devices. Using these platforms reduces cost, improves consistency, and avoids duplication.

The cross-government technical architecture community connects practitioners through Slack channels, regular meetups (architecture lunches and drinks on alternating months), and the Technology in Government blog. The Government Data Architecture Community (GDAC) specifically connects data architects across central and local government.

content.heading: Designing for Interoperability
content.body:
Interoperability means systems can exchange data and use each other's services without bespoke point-to-point integration. In government, where hundreds of systems need to communicate, interoperability is not a nice-to-have — it is the difference between a coherent digital estate and an expensive mess of custom integrations.

The GDS API technical and data standards provide the foundation for interoperable APIs in government. Key principles include: use RESTful API design with JSON as the default data format, use HTTPS for all API communications, implement OAuth 2.0 for API authorisation, version your APIs to avoid breaking consumers, publish API documentation using the OpenAPI specification, and register your API in the government API catalogue.

Beyond API standards, interoperability requires agreement on data semantics — not just the format of data exchange but the meaning of the data exchanged. If one department defines 'address' as a single string and another defines it as structured fields (line 1, line 2, town, postcode), their APIs may technically connect but the data will not be usable without transformation. The government data standards work, coordinated through the Open Standards Board, addresses this by selecting standard representations for common data types.

Architecture patterns for cross-government interoperability include:

Event-driven integration: departments publish events (application submitted, decision made, payment processed) to a shared event infrastructure. Other departments subscribe to events they need. This decouples departments — the publishing department does not need to know who is consuming its events.

API-first design: every service exposes its capabilities through well-documented APIs that follow government standards. Other departments can discover and consume these APIs without bilateral negotiation.

Canonical data models: for frequently shared data (citizen identity, business registration, address), agree on a canonical representation that all departments use. Transform to and from this canonical form at departmental boundaries.

Federated identity: use GOV.UK One Login as the shared identity layer rather than each department maintaining its own identity solution. This eliminates the need for citizens to create separate accounts for each government service.

content.heading: Shared Platforms: When to Use Them and When Not To
content.body:
The Technology Code of Practice principle to 'share and reuse technology' means you should check for existing government platforms before building your own. But this does not mean every service must use every shared platform regardless of fit.

GOV.UK One Login should be your default choice for citizen-facing authentication and identity verification. It provides sign-in with email, password, and two-factor authentication, plus identity verification for services that need it. Services using One Login benefit from citizens only needing one set of credentials across government. However, One Login may not be appropriate for: internal staff systems (where departmental Active Directory or similar is more appropriate), services for professional users with existing sector credentials (solicitors, doctors), or services with security requirements above OFFICIAL.

GOV.UK Notify should be your default choice for sending communications to users — emails, text messages, and letters. It handles delivery, retry logic, and tracking. It is free for government use and supports personalisation, bulk sending, and scheduled delivery. Use it unless you have a genuine requirement that Notify cannot meet (extremely high volume real-time messaging, or integration with existing communication workflows that cannot be modified).

GOV.UK Pay should be your default for collecting payments from citizens. It supports card payments, integrates with government banking arrangements, and handles PCI compliance. Use it unless your service has unusual payment requirements (recurring payments that Pay does not yet support, or very large transaction values that require different processing).

GOV.UK Forms provides a no-code form builder for simple data collection. It is appropriate for straightforward forms that collect information and route it for processing. It may not be appropriate for: complex multi-step journeys with conditional logic, forms that require real-time validation against external data sources, or services that need tight integration with backend processing systems.

The decision framework for shared platforms is: start with the assumption you will use them (the Technology Code of Practice expects this), evaluate whether they meet your specific requirements, document your decision (as an ADR), and if you cannot use a shared platform, articulate why clearly — because assurance will ask. Deviating from shared platforms without good reason is a red flag in both service assessments and digital assurance.

content.heading: The Politics and Practicalities of Cross-Departmental Work
content.body:
Cross-departmental architecture is technically straightforward and organisationally complex. The technical challenges (agreeing APIs, sharing data, integrating systems) are well-understood. The organisational challenges (different priorities, different timelines, different funding, different political pressures) are what actually make cross-government work difficult.

Funding asymmetry is the most common blocker. A cross-government service requires investment from multiple departments. Department A may have the budget and motivation to proceed. Department B may see the benefit but lack funding. Department C may not see sufficient benefit to justify their investment. The architecture must accommodate this reality — designing for incremental adoption where departments can join when they are ready, rather than requiring all participants simultaneously.

Priority misalignment means departments move at different speeds. Your programme may be a top priority in your department but a low priority in the department you depend on. Their team may not be available when you need them. Their API may not be ready when your service needs to go live. Design your architecture to be resilient to dependency delays — use mocks and stubs during development, build fallback mechanisms for when partner services are unavailable, and define clear interface contracts early so teams can develop independently.

Governance complexity multiplies with each department involved. A two-department collaboration needs one shared governance arrangement. A five-department collaboration needs agreement on decision rights, escalation paths, and dispute resolution among five organisations with different governance cultures. The TDC provides a mechanism for cross-government architectural decisions, but programme-level governance still needs to be designed specifically for each collaboration.

Data sharing requires legal gateways. You cannot share personal data between departments just because it would be technically convenient. Each data share requires a legal basis under the Data Protection Act 2018, typically a Data Protection Impact Assessment, and often a formal data sharing agreement. The architect needs to understand these requirements early because they shape what data can flow where — and therefore what the architecture can and cannot do.

Accountability is unclear in cross-departmental work. When a shared service fails, who is accountable? When a cross-government API has a security vulnerability, whose security team responds? Define accountability clearly in the architecture governance — a shared service needs a single accountable owner even if multiple departments use it.

content.heading: Architecture Patterns for Cross-Government Services
content.body:
Several architecture patterns have proven effective for cross-government services.

The Platform Pattern: one department builds and operates a platform that other departments consume as a service. GOV.UK Notify and GOV.UK Pay follow this pattern. The platform team owns the service, sets the API contract, and operates the infrastructure. Consuming departments integrate through documented APIs. This pattern works when one department has the capability and mandate to operate the platform. It fails when the platform team cannot keep up with diverse consumer requirements, or when consuming departments need more control than the platform's standardised interface allows.

The Federation Pattern: each department maintains its own data and services but exposes them through standardised interfaces that allow cross-government queries. Data remains in source systems — it is queried, not replicated. This pattern works for reference data and look-up services where data freshness is important. It fails when cross-government analytics or reporting require aggregated views that cannot be constructed from federated queries.

The Hub Pattern: a central integration hub routes messages, transforms data formats, and manages cross-departmental workflows. Departments connect to the hub rather than to each other directly. This reduces the number of point-to-point integrations from N-squared to N. It works when many departments need to exchange similar data. It fails when the hub becomes a bottleneck or single point of failure, or when the hub team cannot keep pace with onboarding new departments.

The Standards Pattern: no shared infrastructure exists, but all departments agree to follow common standards for data formats, API design, and security protocols. Interoperability is achieved through standards compliance rather than shared platforms. This is the lightest-touch approach and works when departments need to interact infrequently or when the political appetite for shared platforms is low. It fails when standards are not enforced and departments drift into incompatible implementations.

In practice, most cross-government architectures combine patterns. You might use shared platforms for common capabilities (identity, notifications, payments), federation for data sharing, and standards for everything else. The skill is choosing the right pattern for each interaction based on the frequency, criticality, and political feasibility of the integration.

content.heading: Engaging with the Enterprise Architecture Team and TDC
content.body:
The GDS Enterprise Architecture team exists to help departments make better technology decisions that work across government. Engaging with them early — before you have locked in architectural choices — gives you access to: knowledge of what other departments are doing (avoiding duplication), guidance on cross-government standards and patterns, connection to other teams solving similar problems, and visibility of the TDC's strategic direction.

When to engage with the Enterprise Architecture team: when your architecture has cross-departmental implications (your service will be consumed by other departments, or you depend on other departments' services), when you are considering building something that might already exist elsewhere in government, when you are making a technology choice that could set a precedent (the NCR test from spend controls still applies conceptually), or when you need guidance on how to align with cross-government strategy.

The Technical Design Council handles decisions that affect cross-government architecture and shared platforms. If your department is proposing something that would benefit from — or conflict with — cross-government alignment, the TDC is the appropriate escalation point. Proposals to the TDC are submitted as Architecture Decision Records following the cross-government ADR Framework.

Practically, engagement means: joining the cross-government architecture Slack channels, attending the regular architecture community meetups, reading the Technology in Government blog for announcements and direction, and reaching out to the Enterprise Architecture team directly when you have a specific need. The community is collaborative — people share patterns, warn about pitfalls, and connect teams doing similar work.

A common mistake is engaging too late — presenting a fait accompli rather than a question. If you have already committed to an architecture that conflicts with cross-government direction, the conversation becomes difficult. If you engage early and ask 'we are thinking about X — is anyone else doing this? Is there a cross-government position?' you get collaboration rather than conflict.

workedExample.title: Designing a Cross-Government Business Data Sharing Service
workedExample.context: Three departments (Department for Business and Trade, HMRC, and Companies House) need to share reference data about UK businesses to support a new 'tell us once' policy — when a business updates its details with one department, the update should propagate to all three without requiring the business to contact each separately. Each department has its own business data store with different schemas, different identifiers, and different update frequencies. The initiative is politically driven (Blueprint for Modern Digital Government commitment) with ministerial interest.
workedExample.approach:
The Solution Architect from DBT is appointed as the cross-government architecture lead. They must design an architecture that works for all three departments despite different technology stacks and priorities.

Week 1-2 — Discovery across departments:
The architect meets each department's technology team separately to understand their existing systems, data models, and constraints. Key findings: HMRC uses a proprietary customer database with VAT and PAYE numbers as identifiers. Companies House uses a modern API-first platform with company registration numbers. DBT uses a legacy CRM with inconsistent data quality. None of the three systems use the same identifier for the same business.

Week 3-4 — Architecture Options:
The architect develops three options:

Option A (Central Repository): Build a new shared database containing the master record for each business, with all departments writing to and reading from it. Rejected because: no department wants to cede ownership of their data to a central store, data governance becomes impossibly complex, and a single database creates a catastrophic single point of failure.

Option B (Event-Driven Federation): Each department publishes change events when business data is updated. A shared event broker distributes events to subscribing departments. Each department decides what to do with received events — accept the update, queue it for review, or ignore it based on their own business rules. The architect recommends this approach.

Option C (API-Based Polling): Each department exposes an API for querying current business data. Departments periodically poll each other for changes. Simpler to implement but creates latency (changes take hours to propagate) and higher API load.

Week 5-6 — Addressing the Identifier Problem:
The central architectural challenge is: how do you link 'Business X in HMRC's system' to 'Business X in Companies House' when they use different identifiers? The architect proposes a cross-reference service that maintains a mapping between each department's identifier and the Companies House registration number (chosen as the canonical identifier because it is the legal registration).

Week 7-8 — Governance Design:
The architect proposes a lightweight governance model: a monthly cross-department architecture working group (one architect per department), escalation to the TDC for decisions that cannot be resolved between the three departments, and a shared ADR repository for all cross-cutting decisions. Each department retains autonomy over their internal implementation — the shared architecture only governs the interface between departments.
workedExample.outcome: The TDC endorses the event-driven federation pattern and the use of Companies House registration number as the canonical identifier (recorded as a cross-government ADR). Phase 1 delivers a minimum viable integration between Companies House and DBT within 6 months. HMRC joins in phase 2 once their internal systems can publish events. The phased approach accommodates the reality that HMRC's timeline is longer due to internal system complexity.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The critical success factor was not forcing all departments to move at the same pace. The phased approach respected that each department had different readiness levels and different priorities. The event-driven pattern was chosen specifically because it decouples departments — a publishing department does not need to know or care who is consuming its events. The identifier problem was solved pragmatically by choosing an existing government identifier (company registration number) rather than inventing a new one. The governance was kept lightweight because three departments can coordinate without heavy process — more departments would require more structure.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Shared Platform That Nobody Wants to Own
civilServiceScenario.background: Five years ago, three departments collaborated to build a shared document management platform. It was successful initially — all three departments used it, it reduced duplication, and it saved money. But the department that originally operated the platform has undergone a machinery of government change and no longer wants the operational burden. The platform has no dedicated funding — costs were split informally between departments. The technology stack needs upgrading (the containerisation layer is approaching end-of-support). Two of the three departments have grown to depend on it heavily (storing 2 million documents), while the third has migrated to a commercial alternative. Nobody has clear accountability for the platform's future.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You must propose a sustainable future for this platform that addresses the ownership vacuum, secures funding, handles the technology upgrade, and resolves the tension between the departments that depend on it and the one that wants to walk away.
constraints: No single department has budget allocation for the platform
The platform stores 2 million documents, some with retention requirements
The containerisation layer reaches end-of-support in 10 months
The third department's departure reduces the shared funding base by one-third
Two departments have built deep integrations and cannot migrate quickly
There is no formal service level agreement or operational level agreement
The original development team has disbanded — knowledge is limited
GDS has no mandate to adopt departmental platforms as cross-government services
A commercial alternative exists but migration would cost £3 million and take 18 months
The platform has no architectural documentation beyond the original design from 5 years ago
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect in one of the two dependent departments. Your CDIO has asked you to propose options to the cross-departmental steering group.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This scenario illustrates the sustainability problem in cross-government architecture. Shared platforms work well during initial enthusiasm but fail when: original champions move on, funding is not formally secured, and ownership is not clearly assigned. The technical problem (upgrading the container layer) is straightforward — the governance and commercial problem is hard.

Options include: one of the two remaining departments formally adopts the platform as their responsibility (simplest but one department bears disproportionate cost), the two departments jointly fund and govern the platform through a formal agreement (sustainable but requires negotiation), migrate to a commercial managed service (expensive but eliminates the ownership problem), or migrate to a GDS shared platform if one becomes available. The architect's role is presenting these options honestly, with costs and risks, and recommending the most sustainable path — which is probably the formal joint ownership model with clear SLA, cost allocation, and governance.

practiceArtefact.description: Design the integration architecture for a cross-government initiative where DESNZ needs to consume data from three other departments: Companies House (business registration data), HMRC (energy-related tax data), and Ofgem (energy licence data). The integration supports a new energy transition grants service that must verify applicant eligibility by cross-referencing data from all three sources. Produce a high-level integration architecture document.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Consider: what integration pattern is appropriate for each data source (real-time API, batch, event-driven)? How will you handle the fact that each source uses different identifiers? What happens when one source is unavailable? How will you manage data protection requirements (you are combining data from multiple sources about the same entity)? What government standards apply to the API design?
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Cross-Government Integration Architecture: Energy Transition Grants Eligibility**

**Context:** The grants service must verify that an applicant: (1) is a registered UK business (Companies House), (2) meets energy consumption thresholds (HMRC energy tax data), and (3) holds a valid energy licence where required (Ofgem). Verification must complete within 10 seconds of application submission.

**Integration Pattern by Source:**

1. Companies House — Real-time API
Rationale: Companies House provides a well-documented public REST API following government standards. Business registration data is non-sensitive and publicly available.
Approach: Direct API call at application time to verify company registration status and extract registered address.
Fallback: Cache last-known registration status with 24-hour staleness tolerance.

2. HMRC — Batch data share with daily refresh
Rationale: Energy tax data is sensitive (OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE), requires a legal gateway (specific provision in the Energy Act 2023), and HMRC does not provide real-time API access for this data type.
Approach: Daily batch extract of energy consumption aggregates for eligible business categories, loaded into DESNZ secure data store. Eligibility check queries local data store.
Fallback: If daily extract fails, use previous day's data with alert to operations team.
Data protection: DPIA completed, data sharing agreement signed, data minimisation applied (only aggregate consumption bands shared, not detailed transactions).

3. Ofgem — Event-driven with API backup
Rationale: Licence status changes infrequently but must be current. Ofgem publishes licence status change events.
Approach: Subscribe to Ofgem licence status change events to maintain current licence status. API call for initial population and reconciliation.
Fallback: If event stream is interrupted, fall back to API polling every 4 hours.

**Identifier Resolution:**
Canonical identifier: Companies House Registration Number (CRN)
HMRC mapping: maintained via existing HMRC-Companies House cross-reference (VAT number to CRN)
Ofgem mapping: Ofgem licence records include CRN as a mandatory field

**Availability Design:**
Eligibility check is non-blocking — if any source is temporarily unavailable, the application is accepted provisionally and eligibility is confirmed asynchronously within 24 hours. User is notified via GOV.UK Notify.

**Standards Compliance:**
- All APIs follow GDS API technical and data standards
- OAuth 2.0 for service-to-service authorisation
- Mutual TLS for HMRC data channel (sensitive data)
- OpenAPI 3.0 specification for all interface documentation
- Data formatted per government open standards (UTF-8, ISO 8601 dates)

reflectiveQuestions: Think about a cross-departmental initiative you have been involved in. What was the biggest barrier — technical, political, or organisational? How was it resolved (or not)?
How well does your department use GOV.UK shared platforms? Are there services that have built their own notification or payment capabilities rather than using Notify or Pay? Why?
If you needed to propose a cross-government architecture decision to the Technical Design Council, how would you prepare? Who would you need to align with before submitting?
What is the hardest aspect of cross-government data sharing — the legal basis, the technical integration, or getting departments to prioritise the work? Why?
How do you handle the situation where your department's timeline depends on another department's delivery, and that department is not moving as fast as you need?

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the role of the Technical Design Council (TDC) in cross-government architecture?
options: To approve all technology spending across government departments
To make decisions affecting cross-government architecture and shared platforms
To conduct service assessments for cross-departmental services
To manage the GOV.UK shared platform development roadmap
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The TDC is composed of empowered CTOs from across the public sector and is responsible for decisions that affect cross-government architecture and shared platforms. It uses ADRs as its decision mechanism. It does not approve spending (that is now largely devolved under RESET) or conduct assessments.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which integration pattern best supports cross-government services where departments move at different speeds?
options: A shared central database that all departments write to simultaneously
Point-to-point synchronous API calls between all department pairs
Event-driven federation where departments publish events and others subscribe independently
A single monolithic service that replaces all departmental systems
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Event-driven federation decouples departments — a publishing department does not need to know who is consuming its events. This allows departments to join the integration at their own pace without blocking others. It accommodates the reality that different departments have different readiness levels and timelines.

knowledgeCheck.question: According to the Technology Code of Practice, what should you do before building a new capability?
options: Build a prototype immediately to test technical feasibility
Check whether a shared government platform or existing solution already provides the capability
Conduct a formal procurement exercise through the Digital Marketplace
Write a full business case and seek Treasury approval
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The TCoP principle to 'share and reuse technology' means checking for existing solutions before building new ones. This includes GOV.UK shared platforms (One Login, Notify, Pay, Forms), existing departmental platforms that could be extended, and solutions from other departments that could be reused.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most common reason cross-departmental architecture initiatives stall?
options: Technical incompatibility between department systems
Funding asymmetry and priority misalignment between departments
Security requirements preventing data sharing
Lack of available cloud infrastructure
knowledgeCheck.explanation: While technical challenges exist, they are well-understood and solvable. The most common blockers are organisational: one department has budget but another does not, or the initiative is a high priority for one department but low priority for another. Architecture must accommodate this reality by designing for incremental adoption.

knowledgeCheck.question: When should you NOT use a GOV.UK shared platform like Notify or Pay?
options: When your department prefers to use a different vendor
When the shared platform genuinely cannot meet a specific requirement of your service
When your team is more familiar with a different technology
When using the shared platform would be slightly slower to implement
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The TCoP expects you to use shared platforms by default. Deviating requires a genuine requirement that the platform cannot meet — not a preference for something different. If you choose not to use a shared platform, document the decision as an ADR with clear rationale, because assurance will ask why.
